analysis.one_liner: Taxes every stock, bond, and derivatives trade at 0.1 percent to raise federal revenue.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2021 with six Senate sponsors, all Democrats, and was referred to the Finance Committee the day it arrived; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 0.1 percent excise tax on purchases of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded on U.S. exchanges or involving U.S. parties. A $1,000 stock trade would owe $1. New issues of securities would be exempt, so companies raising capital would not pay, and the tax would reach U.S.-owned foreign subsidiaries to prevent trades from being moved offshore. The bill never says what the money would fund; it goes to the Treasury like any other tax.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiary would be the federal Treasury, which would collect a small cut of every covered trade — enough, over time, to be a meaningful revenue source that could fund public priorities. Ordinary investors pay almost nothing directly: $1 per $1,000 trade. The tax falls hardest, proportionally, on firms that trade thousands of times a day.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.1 percent excise tax on purchases of stocks, bonds, and derivatives, so a $1,000 trade owes $1 — a cost borne mostly by firms trading in enormous volume, not by an individual saver making a handful of trades a year.
The tax applies to any trade on a U.S. exchange or involving a U.S. buyer or seller, and to payments on derivatives linked to stocks, debt, commodities, currencies, or indexes.
New issues of securities are exempt, so a company raising money by selling stock or bonds to the public pays nothing — the tax targets the secondary trading market, not business investment.

Trades by controlled foreign corporations owned by U.S. shareholders are covered, and the U.S. owners owe the tax pro rata, closing the easiest route to moving trades offshore; the bill also directs regulators to write rules against avoidance.

Short-term debt with a maturity of 100 days or less is exempt, and the tax does not apply to insurance, annuity, or ordinary business commodity contracts requiring physical delivery — carve-outs aimed at sparing routine commercial activity.

analysis.who_pays: The direct cost falls on trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and asset managers, whose trading margins are often a fraction of a percent. Because the tax is collected on every trade, some of it would be passed through to ordinary investors as slightly higher costs and marginally lower returns in mutual funds and retirement accounts. High-frequency trading volume might also shrink or move to foreign venues despite the bill's anti-avoidance rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-volume traders and large asset managers

drawbacks.text: Because the tax is collected on each purchase — by exchanges and U.S. brokers under the bill — some of the cost would be passed to ordinary investors through mutual funds and retirement accounts, which trade frequently on savers' behalf.
Trading activity that did move to foreign venues not covered by the bill's anti-avoidance rules could reduce the revenue the tax raises and shift some business away from U.S. exchanges.
The bill raises money but never specifies what it would fund, so supporters could not tell voters the revenue was earmarked for anything in particular.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is small for an ordinary investor — $1 per $1,000 traded — and it would raise real revenue from the firms that profit most from high-speed trading. The honest objections are that some cost leaks onto retirement savers through fund trading and that avoidance could erode the take. On balance it is a straightforward tax on financial trading, not a badly designed one: it spares new capital raising, routine commercial hedging, and short-term debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the entire Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2021 on March 18, 2021, joined by Senators Van Hollen, Warren, Gillibrand, Merkley, and Whitehouse.
That same day the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; the action history records no further committee or floor action for the rest of the 117th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill was never taken up again, so the tax was never debated or voted on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-frequency trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and large asset managers kept trading without paying the 0.1 percent tax, and the Treasury forwent the revenue it would have raised. Savers paid nothing, but also got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big trading firms kept the status quo

for.name: Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2021 imposing a 0.1 percent tax on stock, bond, and derivatives trades.

for.name: Chris Van Hollen, Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, Jeff Merkley, and Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in the Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended.

against.name: Securities and financial services industry
against.what_they_did: The securities industry has long opposed financial transaction taxes, and no committee action or floor vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats — 6 of the Senate's 48 Democrats — and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of who opposed it.

industries.note: A tax on every trade hits firms earning thin margins across millions of trades hardest, in proportion to their volume. The bill's main revenue would come out of this trading activity.

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and asset managers
industries.note: These firms would owe the tax on their own trades and would collect it for clients as brokers. Some cost would be passed on to ordinary investors through fund fees and returns.
Exchanges would be responsible for collecting and remitting the tax, an administrative burden, and heavy volume could shrink or move abroad. But the bill does not otherwise regulate them.

industries.industry: Companies raising capital in public markets
industries.note: New issues of securities are exempt, so businesses selling stock or bonds to investors pay nothing. The tax targets secondary trading, not capital formation.
